## 85.63 The Six Are the Next Question

The end of this book is therefore the beginning of another inquiry.

The reader has learned to ask:

> What is the authoritative written Word?

Now he must ask:

> What does that Word teach concerning the first principles of the doctrine of Christ?

The question changes.

The source relationship has been established.

The doctrinal field now opens.

This is the correct transition.

---

## 85.64 The Graphē Has Done Its Work When the Learner Can Enter

The Doctrine of the Graphē succeeds when the learner no longer treats Scripture as merely a collection of religious quotations.

He sees it as authoritative written communication.

He knows that it must be read.

Understood.

Reasoned through.

Handled.

Tested.

Applied.

He knows that his own interpretation remains corrigible.

He knows that the teacher is not the source.

He knows that scholarship is a servant.

He knows that maturity requires work.

He is therefore ready.

That is the point of the gate.

---

## 85.65 The Learner Must Carry the Discipline Forward

The conclusion of this book does not suspend its method.

The learner should carry the method into every course that follows.

When studying repentance, he should use it.

When studying faith, he should use it.

When studying baptisms, he should use it.

When studying laying on of hands, he should use it.

When studying resurrection, he should use it.

When studying eternal judgment, he should use it.

The method does not become a seventh principle.

It becomes a disciplined way of engaging the six principles under the authority of the Graphē.

---

## 85.66 “Study” Is Now a Responsibility

The command of diligence developed in Chapter 78 now becomes concrete.

The learner is not being invited to consume religious information.

He is being called to labour.

He should read.

He should compare.

He should write.

He should reason.

He should test.

He should answer.

He should receive correction.

He should repeat the work until the material becomes skillfully handled.

This is why the Foundation School cannot be reduced to passive content consumption.

The learner must become a workman.

---

## 85.67 The First Principles Require Exercise

The work of Chapter 79 also continues.

The learner must exercise the Word.

He must use what he learns.

He must distinguish.

He must reason.

He must identify errors.

He must explain conclusions.

Repeated responsible use develops capacity.

Therefore the first principles are not merely six headings to memorize.

They are a field in which the learner's faculties are to be exercised.

---

## 85.68 The First Principles Require Maturity

Chapter 80 established that maturity is demonstrated by developed capacity.

That principle continues.

The learner should not assume that knowing the titles of the six principles means understanding them.

Nor does completing a lesson automatically mean possessing mature skill.

The learner must become capable of handling the material.

That is why the foundation is connected to the call to maturity.

---

## 85.69 The First Principles Require Discernment

Chapter 81 examined the babe and the unskilful.

Chapter 82 examined right handling.

Chapter 83 examined the approved workman.

Chapter 84 examined interpretation.

All of that now becomes preparation for the next field.

The learner should enter the Six First Principles with trained discernment.

He should be able to distinguish:

> **what is written**

from:

> **what someone says is written.**

That distinction may determine whether the foundation is laid correctly.

---

## 85.70 The Gate Is Therefore Also a Guard

A gate does two things.

It provides access.

It also regulates access.

The Doctrine of the Graphē does both.

It opens the way to the Six First Principles.

It also warns the learner not to enter them carelessly.

It says:

> Do not make the teacher the source.

> Do not make the institution the source.

> Do not make tradition the source.

> Do not make experience the source.

> Do not make your interpretation the source.

> Do not make the present book the source.

Return to the Graphē.

---

## 85.71 The Gate Prevents Doctrinal Inflation

There is another danger: doctrinal inflation.

A learner can take an explanatory distinction and elevate it into a new doctrine.

He can take a method and call it revelation.

He can take an inference and call it explicit Scripture.

He can take a theological synthesis and call it a direct biblical statement.

He can take a course structure and call it the biblical structure itself.

The Doctrine of the Graphē resists this inflation.

It requires the learner to label what he is doing.

---

## 85.72 Naming the Difference Protects the Truth

Therefore the learner should be willing to say:

> “The text says...”

> “The context indicates...”

> “The necessary inference is...”

> “A reasonable interpretation is...”

> “The broader biblical pattern suggests...”

> “This is an application...”

> “This is a historical observation...”

These distinctions do not weaken doctrine.

They protect it from exaggeration.

---

## 85.73 The Six Principles Should Be Taught With the Same Honesty

When the learner enters the six courses, the same standard applies.

A teacher should not hide a disputed interpretation behind the phrase:

> “The Bible says...”

if the Bible does not say it explicitly.

A teacher should not present an application as though it were a command.

A teacher should not present a theological synthesis as though it were a quotation.

A teacher should not present a possible inference as though it were necessary.

The gate therefore establishes a culture of intellectual honesty.

---

## 85.74 The Graphē Is the Anchor

The course material may change in presentation.

The learner may encounter different teachers.

Different editions may exist.

Translations may differ in wording.

Digital tools may change.

Methods may improve.

Historical scholarship may develop.

But the learner's governing relationship remains:

> **Return to the written Word.**

The Graphē is the anchor.

That is why the title of the present work matters.

One Source of Truth is not a slogan for intellectual simplification.

It identifies the governing written source toward which the learner is repeatedly directed.

---

## 85.75 “One Source” Does Not Mean “One Verse”

The phrase must also be understood carefully.

One source does not mean one verse.

It does not mean one isolated sentence.

It does not mean that every doctrine must be proved by a single quotation.

The Graphē is a body of written testimony.

The workman must handle its passages in context and relation.

One authoritative source can contain many books, voices, genres, contexts, arguments, and witnesses.

Unity of authority does not erase diversity of communication.

---

## 85.76 “One Source” Does Not Mean “One Interpreter”

Nor does one source require one human interpretation.

Human interpreters remain fallible.

The learner should therefore expect discussion, examination, correction, and sometimes disagreement.

The presence of disagreement does not create a second Scripture.

It creates a question of interpretation.

The proper response is to return to the source, examine the reasoning, and assess the evidence.

---

## 85.77 “One Source” Does Not Mean “No Scholarship”

The opposite misunderstanding must also be rejected.

If the Graphē is the primary written authority, it does not follow that scholarship is unnecessary.

The whole of Movement X has established the opposite.

Scholarship is necessary precisely because the source deserves serious labour.

The more authoritative the source is understood to be, the more responsibly it should be handled.

The answer to misuse of Scripture is not less scholarship.

It is better scholarship under the authority of Scripture.

---

## 85.78 The Learner Is Now at the Threshold

The workman has reached the threshold.

Behind him stands the labour of this book.

Before him stand the Six First Principles.

The correct response is neither pride nor fear.

It is readiness.

He should be able to say:

> **I know the source to which I am accountable.**

> **I know that my interpretation is not infallible.**

> **I know that I must labour.**

> **I know that I must distinguish what is written from what I infer.**

> **I know that I must be corrected.**

> **I know that I am now responsible to study the foundation faithfully.**

That is the posture of entry.

---

## 85.79 The Six First Principles Are Entered Under Authority

The learner therefore does not enter the six principles saying:

> “What does my tradition teach?”

He asks:

> **“What does the Graphē establish?”**

He does not begin with:

> “What does my teacher believe?”

He asks:

> **“How does the teacher demonstrate the conclusion from the Word?”**

He does not begin with:

> “What does my experience tell me?”

He asks:

> **“What does Scripture establish, and how should my experience be evaluated in its light?”**

The authority relationship has now become operational.

---

## 85.80 The Foundation School Is Not a Rival to the Graphē

The Foundation School exists to teach the Six First Principles.

It does not replace Scripture.

Its textbook does not replace Scripture.

Its courses do not replace Scripture.

Its exercises do not replace Scripture.

Its teachers do not replace Scripture.

Its assessments do not replace Scripture.

Its certificates do not replace Scripture.

The school is a learning environment.

The Graphē remains the governing written authority.

---

## 85.81 The Six Principles Are Not a Rival to the Graphē

The reverse must also be stated.

The Six First Principles are not an alternative to the Graphē.

They are foundational doctrines identified from the Graphē.

The learner does not choose between:

> **Graphē**

and

> **Six First Principles.**

He moves from:

> **Graphē**

to:

> **understanding what the Graphē teaches concerning the Six First Principles.**

That is the correct relationship.

---

## 85.82 The Difference Between Authority and Content

This distinction can be reduced to two questions.

### Authority

> **What governs the determination of truth?**

The answer in the architecture of this book is the authoritative written Word.

### Content

> **What foundational doctrines are to be studied?**

Hebrews 6:1–2 identifies the Six First Principles.

Authority and content are related.

They are not interchangeable.

The Doctrine of the Graphē concerns the first.

The Foundation School develops the second.

---

## 85.83 The Difference Between Gate and Curriculum

A gate answers:

> **How do you enter?**

A curriculum answers:

> **What do you study once you have entered?**

The Doctrine of the Graphē answers the first question.

The Six First Principles answer the second.

This is why the Graphē should not be counted as a seventh principle.

It performs a different function.

---

## 85.84 The Difference Between Preparation and Progression

Preparation is not the same as progression.

This book has prepared the learner.

The Six First Principles provide the next progression.

The learner should therefore not remain indefinitely in preparation.

At some point, preparation must become study.

Study must become exercise.

Exercise must become skill.

Skill must become maturity.

Maturity must become responsible service.

The gate exists to lead forward.

---

## 85.85 The Difference Between Knowing the Gate and Entering

A person can study the Doctrine of the Graphē and still fail to study the Word.

That would be an irony.

The book would have become an object of intellectual fascination instead of a preparation for faithful engagement.

The correct result is movement.

The learner should leave this work with greater appetite for the Word.

Greater respect for the Word.

Greater responsibility toward the Word.

Greater skill in handling the Word.

And readiness to study what the Word teaches next.

---

## 85.86 The Book Must Create Curiosity, Not Dependency

The conclusion of the manuscript should therefore create curiosity.

The reader should see that the field beyond this gate is substantial.

The Six First Principles are not slogans.

Each opens a serious field of study.

The reader should want to examine them.

But the book should not make the reader dependent upon itself for that examination.

It should send the learner to the next study with a better method and a better relationship to the source.

That is successful completion.

---

## 85.87 The Scholar Becomes the Student Again

The approved workman remains a learner.

The mature learner remains teachable.

The scholar remains accountable.

The person who has studied eighty-five chapters does not graduate from correction.

He becomes more responsible for correction.

He should be able to say:

> “Show me the text.”

> “Show me the reasoning.”

> “Show me the evidence.”

> “Show me where I am wrong.”

This is not insecurity.

It is scholarly integrity.

---

## 85.88 The Foundation Is Entered With Humility

The Six First Principles should therefore be entered with humility.

The learner knows that the first principles are foundational.

He also knows that his understanding of them can be incomplete.

He should not confuse familiarity with mastery.

He should not confuse vocabulary with understanding.

It requires understanding, reasoning, discernment, and right handling.

The student becomes a participant in the work.
